questions.title: Why wasn't this considered "past persecution" when there were death threats, a gunpoint confrontation, an assault on an employee, and an apparent attempted abduction of a child?
questions.question_body: I'm confused about the Tenth Circuit's persecution analysis here. The family got repeated threatening calls, a written death threat, Jimenez was held at gunpoint, armed men later came back looking for him and assaulted an employee, and then a stranger grabbed or at least physically interfered with his son outside school while telling him to run to his dad. The court still says this does not rise to the level of past persecution, especially because there was no lasting physical injury. I thought persecution could be established cumulatively and did not require serious bodily harm. How are courts drawing the line between severe threats/intimidation and legally sufficient persecution in asylum cases?

questions.title: How did the court decide the harm was not "on account of" political opinion when the threats explicitly mentioned the Liberal Party?
questions.question_body: The opinion says the nexus requirement failed because the main reason for the threats was Jimenez's involvement with Don Rafa's property and criminal operations, not the family's political opinion. But some of the threats literally said things like "death to snitches from Liberal Party," and the attackers also described them as people "in politics." I understand mixed-motive cases exist, but I'm having trouble seeing why the political component was only tangential rather than "one central reason." Is the idea that once there is a stronger non-protected motive (like retaliation for investigating criminal activity), the political motive becomes legally insufficient? How do courts evaluate evidence when the persecutor seems to invoke both political affiliation and anti-snitch retaliation?

questions.title: Why did the court treat the 'unable or unwilling to protect' element as unmet when police officers told them to leave because police were part of the problem?
questions.question_body: The family apparently spoke to at least two police officers, and one officer allegedly said nothing could be done and that police officers were contributing to the problem. That sounds to me like evidence of state inability or corruption. But the court says this was only a 'one-off conversation' and that the family made minimal efforts to seek help. What level of reporting or proof is usually required to show a government is unwilling or unable to control private persecutors? Also, if an applicant has reason to think the police are compromised, how much evidence do they need to show that reporting would have been futile or dangerous?

questions.title: Why was internal relocation discussed as if the burden was on the applicants, even though the opinion quotes the government's rebuttal standard?
questions.question_body: The court says the government may rebut a presumption of future persecution by showing the applicant can relocate internally, citing 8 C.F.R. § 1208.13(b)(1)(i). But earlier the court already held there was no past persecution, so there was no presumption to rebut. Then in the relocation section the court says the petitioners 'have not demonstrated' a fear of future persecution, but 'even if they had,' the record supports relocation. I'm confused about who bears the burden on internal relocation when there is no finding of past persecution. Is the burden on the asylum applicant to prove relocation is unreasonable, or on DHS to prove relocation is reasonable? Did the court just discuss relocation as an alternative holding?

questions.title: What does it mean that the court reviewed the BIA's decision but could still 'consult the IJ's more complete explanation'?
questions.question_body: On the standard of review, the court says that because a single BIA member affirmed the IJ, it reviews the BIA's decision, but it is not precluded from consulting the IJ's fuller reasoning. Procedurally, I'm not sure how this works. If the BIA affirms and adds some discussion of its own, is the court reviewing only the grounds expressly adopted by the BIA, or can it rely on any rationale from the IJ? What are the limits on a circuit court using the IJ's opinion when the BIA issues a streamlined or brief affirmance?

questions.title: Why did the withholding of removal claim automatically fail just because the asylum claim failed?
questions.question_body: At the end, the court says that because the petitioners failed to demonstrate a well-founded fear of persecution for asylum, they necessarily failed to meet the higher standard for withholding of removal. I thought withholding and asylum overlap a lot, but are not identical, especially because asylum is discretionary and withholding is mandatory if the standard is met. Is the court saying withholding always fails whenever asylum fails, or only when asylum fails on certain merits elements like persecution/nexus/government protection rather than timing, discretion, or procedural bars?

questions.title: Did the court effectively treat the particular social group theory as waived because it was not developed on appeal?
questions.question_body: The opinion notes that the petitioners argued nexus based on both political opinion and particular social group, but then says they did not brief the existence of any particular social group or establish membership in one, so the court limited review to political opinion. I'm trying to understand the appellate practice point here. In immigration petitions for review, how much development is required to preserve a PSG argument? If the issue was raised before the IJ and BIA but only mentioned in passing in the circuit brief, is that considered forfeited or waived?
